copla.window: 1917 onward (El Relicario, 1917, is called the first copla; the form took shape in the 1920s out of cuplé, tonadilla, zarzuela and ópera flamenca; it flourished in the 1930s and 1940s and in 1950s musical film, was displaced by pop and the romantic ballad in the 1960s, and is still sung)
copla.sound: Spain's dramatic popular song of the variety stage and the musical film: one singer with a powerful, vibrato-rich voice, usually in an Andalusian accent and flamenco-coloured but without the depth of cante jondo, tells a short story of passion, jealousy or ruin over a theatre orchestra. Much of it was written by the trio Quintero, León and Quiroga, in pasodoble, zambra, tango or bolero rhythms.
markers: A theatre orchestra, not a lone guitar, with long introductions and dramatic pauses
A big, controlled voice with strong vibrato, flamenco-tinged but not deep cante
Short, story-telling lyrics of overflowing love, betrayal, jealousy and sorrow
Pasodoble, zambra, tango or bolero rhythms under the same singers
near: The band pasodoble: an instrumental march for wind band, with no singer and no story; copla borrows the rhythm but is sung theatre song
Flamenco cante (fandangos) with guitar from a cantaora: free, deep cante jondo, not an orchestral copla
